tldr: We present FAME-QP, a GPU-native QP solver that solves dense quadratic programs arising in linear MPC at ultra-high speed through GPU kernel fusion and constraint-dependent operator optimization. It achieves significantly lower latency than existing GPU solvers, enabling 2 ms cycle control of a humanoid robot and online trajectory tracking for a quadrotor.
hero_caption: A disturbance response experiment on the humanoid robot Unitree G1 in the MuJoCo simulation environment. Even when subjected to a strong 80 N impact to the torso (red arrow) that causes a large tilt, fast MPC powered by FAME-QP at a 2 ms cycle quickly restores the upright posture without falling.
overview:
Model predictive control (MPC) is an exceptionally powerful tool for real-time robot control. However, solving constrained optimization problems—specifically quadratic programs (QPs)—within tight control cycles of a few milliseconds or less is challenging. In recent years, integration with massively parallel GPU computing and learning-based world models has advanced rapidly. Yet, relying on conventional CPU-based QP solvers creates a severe bottleneck due to the latency of data transfers between the CPU and GPU.

To tackle this, the authors developed FAME-QP, a dense QP solver that keeps all computations entirely on the GPU and trims latency to the absolute minimum. The baseline algorithm is ADMM (alternating direction method of multipliers), which is naturally parallelizable. FAME-QP supercharges it with hardware-oriented techniques: it compresses operator sizes by exploiting box constraint structures, fuses updates into one or two kernels, and replays them through CUDA graphs. It also introduces a probing mechanism across a cached operator bank to choose the initial penalty parameter, along with a lazy update strategy when problem matrices change.

For validation, alongside random QP benchmarks, the authors conducted simulations of a 2 ms push recovery on the 29-joint Unitree G1 humanoid and trajectory tracking on a quadrotor whose model matrices change at every step. FAME-QP achieved speedups ranging from several-fold to over ten-fold compared to state-of-the-art GPU solvers such as CuPIQP and ReLU-QP, while demonstrating high tracking accuracy and stability.
contributions: Introduced constraint-dependent operator representations exploiting diagonal box structures, reducing operator memory by up to 4x and speeding up iteration times by up to 3x compared to fully dense formulations.
Fused ADMM iterations into single- or two-kernel executions replayed via CUDA graphs, minimizing host-device communication overhead with automated execution configuration based on device profiling.

Proposed an initial penalty selection strategy by probing a precomputed penalty operator bank, along with a lazy update mechanism that defers matrix inversions until needed when problem matrices change.
Demonstrated real-time control with significantly lower latency than existing GPU solvers on a 2 ms MPC task for a humanoid and on quadrotor Koopman MPC with time-varying matrices.

sections.heading: Why Do We Need a GPU-Native QP Solver Now?
sections.summary: Real-time robot MPC demands millisecond-level QP solving speed. As simulation and learning pipelines move to GPUs, an ultra-fast GPU-resident QP solver is essential to eliminate CPU-GPU data transfer overhead.
sections.details:
In robot control, linear model predictive control (LMPC) is formulated as a convex quadratic program (QP). To operate real hardware safely, this QP must be solved reliably within each control cycle (often just a few milliseconds).

Representative algorithms for solving QPs include interior-point (IP) methods, active-set (AS) methods, and operator-splitting (OS) methods such as the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM). While interior-point methods require few iterations, their linear system solves per step are heavy, and warm-starting is challenging. Active-set methods risk combinatorial explosion as constraint counts grow. In contrast, ADMM is well suited for robot control where moderate accuracy suffices; it warm-starts easily and maps naturally to parallel hardware.

Modern robotics increasingly runs learning-based world models and parallel simulations on GPUs. However, keeping the optimization solver on the CPU forces frequent data ping-pong between the CPU and GPU, introducing transfer latencies that jeopardize real-time deadlines. To address this, the authors propose FAME-QP (Fused ADMM with Multimode Execution for QP solution), a solver that keeps all data on the GPU to solve dense QPs with ultra-low latency.

sections.heading: How Does It Compare to Prior GPU Solvers?
sections.summary: Existing GPU QP solvers based on iterative or interior-point methods suffer from dispatch overhead and operator redundancy. FAME-QP resolves these bottlenecks by combining pre-inverted operator banks, slimmed operators, kernel fusion, and lazy updates.
sections.details:
### Evolution of GPU QP Solvers
Prior efforts to solve QPs on GPUs include cuOSQP, which parallelizes the indirect linear solver in OSQP, and interior-point implementations like qpax and CuPIQP. Although CuPIQP utilizes kernel fusion and CUDA graphs, the inherent computational weight of interior-point iterations remains demanding in certain settings. The closest approach to this work is ReLU-QP. ReLU-QP conceptualizes ADMM iterations as a weight-tied neural network, caching pre-inverted operators for penalty adaptation. However, it treats operators as completely dense matrices—wasting memory—suffers from kernel launch overhead on each iteration, and struggles when problem matrices vary online.

### Contrast with GPU Parallelization at the Optimal Control Level
Approaches like MPCGPU and TurboMPC implement sequential quadratic programming (SQP) on GPUs for nonlinear MPC, while frameworks like CUDA MPC and pi-MPC exploit horizon-level parallelism. These methods are tailored to specific problem structures. In contrast, FAME-QP directly takes condensed, general dense convex QPs and flexibly handles online matrix changes, positioning it as a general-purpose QP solver.

sections.heading: The Fundamentals: ADMM for QPs and Condensed MPC
sections.summary: We review the convex QP formulation, the condensed MPC representation that eliminates state variables to keep only inputs, and the closed-form ADMM updates and termination criteria.
sections.details:
### ADMM Formulation for Quadratic Programs
The target problem is a convex QP with cost function $1/2 z^\top P z + q^\top z$ and constraints $l \leq G z \leq h$. In ADMM, an auxiliary variable $s$ is introduced to split the problem into $Gz = s$ and $l \leq s \leq h$. Constructing the augmented Lagrangian with regularization parameter $\sigma$ and diagonal penalty matrix $\bm{\rho}$, updates for each iteration can be computed in closed form.

Specifically, by precomputing the inverse $M = K^{-1}$ of the matrix $K = P + \sigma I + G^\top \bm{\rho} G$, the primal variable update reduces to simple matrix-vector multiplications. Updating the slack variables requires only element-wise clipping (box projection) between lower and upper bounds, making it exceptionally well-suited for parallel execution on GPUs.

### Condensed Formulation of LMPC (Condensed QP)
Using the state-space model $x_{k+1} = A x_k + B u_k$, predicted states $x$ are recursively expressed in terms of inputs $u$, eliminating all state variables from the decision variables. This is known as "condensing." The number of decision variables shrinks to $n = N n_u$, the product of the prediction horizon $N$ and input dimension $n_u$, producing a compact, dense matrix structure. This dense format matches GPU tensor operations and parallel multiply-accumulate units exceptionally well.

sections.heading: FAME-QP's Core Techniques: Five Smart Optimizations
sections.summary: We examine the five key mechanisms: constraint-dependent operator representations, single- and two-kernel fusion, automated mode selection via hardware profiling, penalty bank probing, and lazy updates during model changes.
sections.details:
FAME-QP is tailor-made to execute ADMM iterations on GPUs at maximum speed.

### Slimming Operators via Constraint Structures
The constraint matrix $G$ is not always fully dense. Constraints can be categorized into "box" (diagonal, input bounds only), "split" (diagonal input bounds plus general state constraints), and "general" constraints. FAME-QP absorbs diagonal blocks into element-wise operations without storing useless zero entries in memory. This reduces operator footprint by up to 4x compared to storing everything as dense matrices.

### Two Operator Formats and Kernel Fusion
For iteration computation, FAME-QP provides two options: a "stacked" format that updates primal and slack variables simultaneously via a single large matrix-vector product, and a "factored" format that splits updates into two stages. The stacked format runs the entire iteration in a "single fused kernel" using inter-block synchronization, shared memory, and registers. The factored format uses a "two-kernel" sequence, reducing memory traffic.

### Eliminating CPU Overhead with CUDA Graphs
To remove per-iteration kernel launch latency, dozens of iteration kernels and termination checks are captured into a "CUDA graph" and replayed. The CPU host only needs to inspect a few residual values at periodic intervals, driving dispatch latency close to zero.

### Hardware-Calibrated Automated Mode Selection
Balancing problem dimensions, GPU memory bandwidth, and kernel launch overhead, FAME-QP profiles whether the stacked (single-kernel) or factored (two-kernel) mode is faster. It selects the winner based on empirical timing with placeholder data rather than purely theoretical models.

### Penalty Bank Probing and Lazy Updates
ADMM convergence depends heavily on the penalty parameter $\rho$. FAME-QP maintains a bank of pre-inverted operators for five distinct values of $\rho$. During setup, it runs brief test iterations (probing) to pick the best initial penalty. Furthermore, when matrices $P$ or $G$ change during robot operation, instead of immediately inverting all bank entries, it updates only the currently active operator and defers the rest until needed. This "lazy update" cuts online computation overhead roughly in half.

sections.heading: Experimental Results: Ultra-Low Latency and Closed-Loop Control
sections.summary: FAME-QP outperformed existing GPU and CPU solvers on random QP benchmarks. It also achieved high control performance on a 2 ms push-recovery task for a humanoid and 3D trajectory tracking for a quadrotor with time-varying model matrices.
sections.details:
### Numerical Benchmarks: Random QPs and LMPC
Benchmarking on an NVIDIA RTX 3080 Laptop GPU compared FAME-QP against representative state-of-the-art solvers. On random QP problems with matched accuracy (solution error within $10^{-3}$ of Clarabel), FAME-QP (float64) achieved 1.2x to 25.9x speedups over the fastest CPU solver (DAQP) and 1.5x to 4.3x speedups over the fastest GPU solver (ReLU-QP) across all sizes $n \ge 220$. In single precision (float32), it solved an $n=1400$ problem in just 1.95 ms (compared to 326 ms for cuOSQP).

In a 50-step closed-loop MPC simulation on unstable systems (TABLE I), FAME-QP recorded average step times between 0.658 ms and 4.23 ms. This was 3.2x to 7.3x faster than its competitor ReLU-QP, and 3.2x to 13.8x faster than the MPC-tailored $\pi$MPC solver.

### Unitree G1 Humanoid Push Recovery (2 ms Control Loop)
Center-of-mass and joint control for the 29-joint Unitree G1 humanoid was evaluated at an ultra-fast 2 ms control cycle. Under an 80 N lateral push disturbance, ReLU-QP exceeded the 2 ms budget when the prediction horizon reached $N \ge 15$. FAME-QP, however, solved the problem in an average of 1.40 ms even at $N=20$, comfortably meeting the real-time deadline. It kept the CoM RMS deviation to roughly 19 mm, successfully recovering balance.

### Quadrotor Koopman MPC (Online Matrix Updates)
In a task where a Skydio X2 quadrotor tracks a figure-8 (lemniscate) trajectory, Koopman linearization causes the QP cost and constraint matrices to change at every step. Because matrix recomputation is required, ReLU-QP cannot run this task directly. Leveraging its lazy updates, FAME-QP solved each step in an average of 12.5 ms (17.6 ms at the 99th percentile), strictly adhering to the 20 ms (50 Hz) control limit. It achieved a 4.7x speedup over CuPIQP (mean 59.2 ms) with a precise tracking RMSE of 2.7 mm.

### Insights from Ablation Studies
Ablation experiments isolating each component revealed that combining kernel fusion with CUDA graph replay drastically slashed iteration time from $140\,\mu\mathrm{s}$ down to $4.37\,\mu\mathrm{s}$. Furthermore, constraint structure separation reduced memory footprint by up to 4x, and penalty probing reduced iteration counts by 1.6x to 3.2x, confirming that each module contributes synergistically.

The red solid line is the reference trajectory, and the yellow dashed line is the flight path with FAME-QP. Even with matrix updates at every time step, it consistently computes optimal solutions in real time and tracks the path accurately.

sections.heading: Summary and What Lies Ahead
sections.summary: By unifying constraint-aware operators, kernel fusion, CUDA graphs, penalty probing, and lazy updates, FAME-QP minimizes latency for dense MPC QPs. Future work aims to expand into sparse formulations and horizon-level structures.
sections.details:
FAME-QP is designed to extract maximum parallel performance from GPUs for dense quadratic programs arising in linear MPC. Beyond algorithmic formulations, detailed hardware-conscious optimizations—targeting caches, memory bandwidth, and launch overhead—create decisive speed advantages for real-time robotic control.

While this work focused primarily on condensed, dense QP formulations, the authors point toward future directions: incorporating sparse formulations that retain state variables and leveraging block parallelism across the horizon to improve scalability for even larger problems.

takeaways: In accelerating GPU solvers for millisecond- and microsecond-critical MPC, eliminating launch overhead via CUDA graph replay and kernel fusion is just as crucial as algorithmic parallelism.
Separating the diagonal structure of box constraints from dense matrices slashes operator memory by up to 4x and accelerates memory-bandwidth-bound GPU computations by up to 3x.
For problems where matrices change at every step, lazy updates that defer unused operator inversions cut the online update burden roughly in half.
limitations: The current implementation is built around condensed formulations (dense QPs) where state variables are eliminated; for very large problems with long prediction horizons or high input dimensions, memory and compute demands may grow faster than in sparse solvers.
Because setup involves penalty probing and device calibration, it is tailored for repetitive MPC tasks solving thousands of similarly structured QPs rather than isolated one-off QP solves.
In single precision (float32), residuals tend to plateau around $10^{-6}$; double precision (float64) remains necessary for tasks demanding high numerical accuracy.
